name: Nora Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me is confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four, and by five I'm in the milking parlour at Holloway's with Pete, the herdsman. Sixty-two cows, and I'm still slower than him at getting the clusters on, that's the cups that go on the teats. After milking it's the calves, scraping out the yard, then whatever Mr Holloway needs in the barley. I love the calves. My knees love none of it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming at 58?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did twenty-six years in the kitchen at Brookfield primary school, and when the council handed school meals to a catering firm they cut half of us. There's nothing round here but farms and the feed mill, so I asked at Holloway's and they took me on at the bottom rate. My Arne drove buses till his back went, so it's his small pension and my wage, and most months there's nothing left by the 28th. I kept my union card from the school days and moved it over to the farmworkers' branch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds like most things people get excited about. A lot of fuss and then the same muck to shovel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say in the break room: told you so. Every year someone's selling Mr Holloway a gadget that'll change everything, and the cows still need milking at five. I'd probably say it at the union branch too, because they've been worried about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix anything for me. My problem isn't robots, it's that I'm on the lowest rate on the farm and the rent went up again in September. Plateau or no plateau, I'm still counting coins at the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep doing my shifts and keep asking Pete to show me the things I'm slow at, like spotting when a cow's coming into heat. Maybe I'd finally pay off the last 60 on the washing machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, I suppose. Not happy, because steady for me means tight, but there's nothing new to be scared of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the union branch has been worried. What were they worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a dairy two valleys over that put in milking robots, the kind where the cow walks in by herself and a machine arm does the lot. Three milkers went down to one. Gwen, our branch secretary, keeps saying we need rules on it before it spreads, and I agree with her, though I've never seen one of those machines up close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, what do the next few years look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milking till my knees give up, and hoping that's after 66, when the state pension comes in. Arne and I worked it out on the back of an envelope once, and we'd scrape by on two pensions if the rent doesn't climb again. That's the whole plan. It's not a big one.

S0.say: I'd say told you so in the break room: every year someone sells the boss a gadget and the cows still need milking at five. I'd say the same at the union branch.
S0.think: I'd be relieved, but it doesn't fix anything for me. I'm on the lowest rate on the farm and the rent just went up, so I'm still counting coins either way.
S0.do: Keeps working her shifts and asks the herdsman to teach her what she's slow at, like spotting a cow in heat. Pays off the last 60 she owes on the washing machine.
S0.feel: Steady but tight. Nothing new to fear, but nothing to be happy about either.
S0.quote: Plateau or no plateau, I'm still counting coins at the till.
S0.fieldNote: Nora frames everything around money, not technology: the September rent rise matters more to her than any machine. Her union loyalty came with her from the school kitchen and shapes how she talks in public. She knows about milking robots only second-hand, through the branch secretary, and says so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I can actually picture, because it's already started with those milking robots. That's the one that would reach Holloway's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the branch I'd say we need an agreement before any machine comes in: who stays, who gets trained, what happens to the ones who don't. I don't post online, so nobody would hear from me there. To Pete I'd say we stick together on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I know who goes first, and it's me. Pete knows every cow by name and Mr Holloway's son can fix anything with an engine, and I'm the 58-year-old who still fumbles the clusters. If a robot comes in, the newest and slowest hand is the one they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to Gwen the same week and ask for a meeting with Mr Holloway before anything gets bought. I'd stop the little extras, the Friday chips with Arne and the gardening magazine, and try to put 20 a week aside. I wouldn't learn the robot, I'll be honest. I can barely work the timer on the oven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, if I'm truthful. It's the school kitchen all over again, a nice letter and a handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the robot. If Mr Holloway offered to train you on it, would you really say no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's fair, you've caught me there. I'd go to the training, because I'd be daft to refuse with the rent what it is. But I'd sit at the back and be the one who doesn't get it, and they'd know it by the second day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Liv is a nurse in the city and she'd tell me to stop worrying and move near her. I wouldn't tell her the half of it. A mother doesn't phone her daughter to say she can't make the rent at 58.

S1.say: I'd tell the union branch we need an agreement before any machine comes in, covering who stays and who gets trained. I'd tell the herdsman we stick together.
S1.think: I'm sure I'd go first, because I'm the newest and slowest hand on the farm. The herdsman and the farmer's son have skills a robot can't replace, and I don't.
S1.do: Asks the branch secretary for a meeting with the farmer before any robot is bought. Cuts small treats and tries to save 20 a week, and would attend training on a robot if offered while expecting to struggle.
S1.feel: Sick to her stomach. It brings back losing her school kitchen job.
S1.quote: A mother doesn't phone her daughter to say she can't make the rent at 58.
S1.fieldNote: Nora had already worked out the order of who would be let go and put herself first. She said she wouldn't learn the robot, then admitted she'd go to training but expected to fail by the second day. She'd hide the worst from her daughter out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be 60. That's not long enough to do anything except watch it come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why government has to step in, with a proper income for people pushed out, paid for by the firms selling the robots. I'd march if Gwen organised one and sign every petition that came round. I'd say it to anyone at the feed mill who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd be finished at Holloway's inside a year of it arriving, maybe sooner. Two years isn't warning for someone like me. I can't save my way through it when I save nothing, and I can't learn a new trade at 60 when I'm still learning this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before it arrives, I'd go to every meeting and every march, and I'd be at Councillor Moss's office asking what the plan is. I'd sell Arne's old car, cancel the TV package and stop pretending we don't need the food bank at the church hall. The day I'm let go I'd be at the benefits office that afternoon. I'm not too proud, I paid my taxes for forty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened, the kind where you lie awake at three doing sums that never come out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would go unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council tax, because they let you fall behind a bit before they come knocking. Then the phone. The rent's the last thing I'd let slip, because once you lose the house at our age you don't get another one round here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years' warning change things for you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years there's no getting to 66, that's the whole thing. I've got eight years to my pension, and if the work goes in two, that's six years of nothing in the middle. Give me ten and I'd nearly be over the line.

S2.say: I'd say government has to step in with a proper income for people pushed out, paid for by the firms selling the robots. I'd march and sign every petition going.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the farm within a year of it arriving. I can't save my way through because I save nothing, and I can't learn a new trade at 60.
S2.do: Joins every union meeting and march, and presses the local councillor for a plan. Sells the old car, cancels the TV package and uses the church food bank, then applies for benefits the day she's let go.
S2.feel: Properly frightened, lying awake at three doing sums that never come out.
S2.quote: I've got eight years to my pension, and if the work goes in two, that's six years of nothing in the middle.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Nora broke. She did the pension arithmetic out loud: eight years to go, six of them possibly with no wage. In public she demands state support paid for by the companies, and in private she's ready to use the food bank and benefits without shame. The timing, more than the technology, is what frightens her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be 63. Still short, but closer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: government needs to plan for this now, not wait for it to land. I'd say five years is plenty of time for them to sort out an income for people like us, so there's no excuse. At work I'd tell the younger ones to get their names down for any training going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63, which is three years short of the pension. Three years you can maybe get through on odd jobs and Arne's money, if nothing else goes wrong. It's still a hole, just a smaller one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting something by, even 15 a week, in the biscuit tin, because I don't trust banks with small money. I'd ask the branch what the rules are for taking a pension early at 63. And I'd stay at Holloway's as long as they'd have me, every shift they offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not the cold sweat of the two-year one. More like the feeling before a dentist appointment you can't cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you time to see it coming. What would you be watching for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salesman. When the man from the machinery dealer starts having tea in Mr Holloway's kitchen every month, I'll know. Pete says the dealer already came once in the summer with brochures, and I pretended not to notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about any other kind of work in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe going back to a kitchen, if there's one left that a robot hasn't got. But there's only the pub and the care home in our village, and the care home already turned me down once. I'm not choosing between jobs, I'm hoping one doesn't close.

S3.say: I'd say government has five years to plan an income for people like us, so there's no excuse. I'd tell the younger workers to sign up for any training going.
S3.think: Five years gets me to 63, three years short of my pension. That's a gap I might survive on odd jobs and my partner's pension, if nothing else goes wrong.
S3.do: Starts saving 15 a week in a biscuit tin and asks the union about taking her pension early at 63. Takes every shift the farm offers for as long as they'll keep her.
S3.feel: Worried, like waiting for a dentist appointment she can't cancel, but not in a cold sweat.
S3.quote: When the man from the machinery dealer starts having tea in Mr Holloway's kitchen every month, I'll know.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Nora's fear shrank to a specific number: a three-year gap before her pension. She'd save in a tin because she doesn't trust banks with small sums. Her early-warning sign is concrete and local, the machinery dealer's visits. She sees almost no other work in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 68 and drawing my pension. That's a different picture altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still say it's wrong and it needs rules, because it's not about me, it's about the young ones coming up. Liv's boy is twelve and wants to work with animals. I'd say that at the branch and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I'm honest, ten years mostly misses me. I'd be out of it by the time it arrives, so it's my grandson I'd lie awake about. Selfishly, there's a bit of relief in that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Holloway's and keep going to branch meetings, nothing dramatic. I'd keep the tin going and talk to Liv about her boy's schooling, whether animal work is still a good idea. Mostly I'd wait and see what happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for me, guilty about the relief, and worried for my grandson.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there's a bit of relief. Can you say more about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a horrible thing to admit. I've spent my whole life being the one things happen to: the kitchen, the rent, the knees. For once the wave would come after I'm already out of the water, and I'd be lying if I said that didn't feel nice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your grandson about working with animals?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to do it if he loves it, but to learn the machines too, which is rich coming from me. And I'd tell him to join the union on day one. That's the only advice I know works.

S4.say: I'd still say it's wrong and needs rules, because it's about the young ones coming up, not me. My grandson wants to work with animals.
S4.think: Ten years mostly misses me, because I'd be 68 and on my pension. It's my grandson I'd lie awake about, and there's a selfish relief in that.
S4.do: Carries on at the farm, keeps going to branch meetings and keeps saving in the tin. Talks to her daughter about whether animal work is still a good path for her grandson, and otherwise waits to see what happens.
S4.feel: Relieved for herself, guilty about the relief, and worried for her grandson.
S4.quote: For once the wave would come after I'm already out of the water, and I'd be lying if I said that didn't feel nice.
S4.fieldNote: The ten-year picture lands after her state pension, and that changes everything for Nora. She openly admitted relief and then guilt about it. Her worry moved to her grandson, and she caught the irony of telling him to learn the machines she won't touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. It's not the robots, it's the gap between losing the work and getting my pension. What would help is a bridge, some kind of guaranteed income for people over 55 until the pension starts, and an agreement at the farm that nobody gets let go without notice and a payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Arne. Everyone asks about the worker, never the one at home. If I lose Holloway's, it's his little pension feeding two, and he wore his back out for that money.

headlineQuote: It's the school kitchen all over again, a nice letter and a handshake.
portrait: Nora Larsen is 58 and has milked cows at Holloway's dairy and barley farm for three years, after the council outsourced the school kitchen where she worked for twenty-six. She's on the bottom rate, still slower than the herdsman, and lives with Arne, a former bus driver with a bad back and a small pension. She carried her union card from the kitchen to the farm and believes rules and public support are the answer. She expects to be first out if machines arrive, and the two-year AGI picture frightened her most because it leaves years with no wage before her pension. With ten years' warning she felt relief, then guilt, and turned her worry to her grandson.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because losing her farm work at 60 would leave about six years without a wage before her state pension at 66.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for people over 55 until their pension starts, and an agreement at the farm that nobody is let go without notice and a payment.
